title: Research Before You Buy: A Practical Property Due-Diligence Framework
videoTitle: RESEARCH WORK REQUIRED BEFORE BUYING A PROPERTY
excerpt: A repeatable way to test an address, its real market tier, comparable prices and rental demand before committing to a property.
takeaways: Define the exact micro-market instead of accepting a premium neighbourhood label from an advertisement.
Compare like with like: the correct area tier, recent transactions, and new homes against an appropriate new-home benchmark.
An investment property should have more than one realistic rental strategy and a clear break-even plan.

sections.heading: Map the real address
paragraphs: Sean begins with a deceptively simple requirement: know the location inside out. Neighbourhood branding can blur meaningful boundaries, especially when a project borrows the name of a nearby premium address. Two homes five minutes apart may attract different residents, support different rents and sit in very different price bands.

Research should therefore start with roads, access points, employment centres, transport links and the people who actually choose to live there. A future commercial district or rail connection can strengthen demand, but the buyer still needs to identify who will pay rent and why that tenant would choose this address over the alternatives.

sections.heading: Build the right comparison set
paragraphs: A nearby launch is not automatically a valid price benchmark. Sean separates prime and local-market tiers, then separates newer and older stock within those tiers. The useful question is whether the asking price makes sense beside recent transactions for genuinely comparable homes, rather than whether another developer is asking even more.

Newer buildings can command a premium through layouts, facilities and condition, but that premium still needs evidence. If a new project can be bought close to the transacted price of older alternatives in the same demand area, the proposition becomes easier to defend. If the gap is large, the buyer needs a strong reason for paying it.

sections.heading: Stress-test demand and the exit
paragraphs: Sean prefers investments with multiple ways to reach break-even. Depending on the location, those routes might include a conventional family tenancy, shorter corporate stays or room rental. The correct options come from observed demand; a strategy that works in one district may perform poorly a few kilometres away.

Before signing, write down the target tenant, achievable rent, operating costs and at least one fallback. Then ask what happens if the promised infrastructure is delayed, the preferred rental model weakens or competing supply arrives. Research earns its value when it exposes those weak points before the loan begins.

closing: A convincing brochure explains the project. Proper due diligence explains the market around it, the price you are paying and the demand that must support your decision.
